## Understand the actual problem

**LeetCode 239 — Sliding Window Maximum.**

Keep a deque of candidate indices, not all window elements. Remove expired indices from the front and remove smaller dominated values from the back.

## First try the obvious approach

Compute the maximum of each k-length window by scanning all k entries; this repeats most comparisons when neighbouring windows overlap.

The goal is not to memorise a data structure. It is to identify which partial result the next operation can reuse.

## Mathematical relationship, explained immediately

$$
a_{q_0}\geq a_{q_1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{q_m}
$$

**Symbol by symbol:** q₀ through q_m are indices kept in the deque from front to back; the corresponding values are nonincreasing, so the front index holds the current maximum.

**Calculate with real numbers:** For values [1,3,−1] with window k=2, after processing 1 the deque contains [1]. Adding 3 removes 1 as dominated, leaving [3]; window [1,3] max is 3. Adding −1 leaves [3,−1], so window [3,−1] max remains 3.

Read the equation and the calculation as one explanation. If the numbers do not make sense, do not skip ahead to code.

## How the algorithm emerges

1. Identify what answer you would compute by hand for the smallest instance.
2. Store exactly that piece of information when moving to the next step.
3. Update the stored information after one input event or query.
4. Check the invariant before returning a result; consider boundary values and ties.

**Correctness argument:** Any smaller value before a later larger value can never again be a maximum while the later larger value stays in the window. Removing it cannot change any future answer.

## Code, but only after the reasoning

Use the tested [algorithm lab](../examples/patterns.mjs), which exports `slidingWindowMax`:

~~~js
import { slidingWindowMax } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(slidingWindowMax([1,3,-1,-3,5],3));
~~~

Run this code from a `.mjs` file in the current topic folder. The [automated tests](../examples/patterns.test.mjs) include small examples and boundary cases.

## Count the work rigorously

**Time and memory:** O(n) time and O(k) active deque space where n is input length and k window width.

**The misleading shortcut:** The deque must store indices so expiry can be checked. Merely storing values cannot tell whether the front occurrence has left the window.

A common interview error is to mistake a nested loop for quadratic complexity. For a monotonic stack/queue, one item is removed at most once, so total work is linear. Conversely, a sorted data structure is not automatically fast for every possible operation.
